title: Rubio Says US-India Trade Deal Will Happen Shortly During Mumbai Visit
excerpt: Marco Rubio said the two countries are as close as they can be without an executed agreement, after months of stalled talks over tariffs and Russian oil.
body:
• U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in Mumbai on October 20 that a U.S.-India trade deal will happen shortly, with only a small number of items left to wrap up.
  • Rubio said the two sides are about as close as they can be without having an executed agreement, and hoped for good news to announce fairly soon, followed by a signing by the leaders.
  • The Associated Press reported the talks have been stalled for months, after tariffs of up to 50% in August 2025 were cut to 18% under a February 2026 framework that then stalled.
  • For Indian exporters and U.S. importers, nothing changed on Tuesday itself; the rate and terms will only be known when the remaining items are settled and the deal is announced.

A trade deal between the United States and India will happen shortly, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on arriving in India on Tuesday (October 20, 2026). Speaking to reporters in Mumbai, Rubio said the two countries were very, very close to an agreement, with a small number of items left to finish, The Times of India reported.

https://x.com/ETNOWlive/status/2112502168167289234

"We're very, very close. I would say we're about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement. I think there's a small number of items left to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly."

— Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State

Rubio was careful about his own role. He said the State Department does not negotiate trade agreements, but that it is very much involved, and that he and his counterpart, the National Security Advisor, care a lot about it. He hoped for good news to announce fairly soon, with the leaders signing it thereafter.

Rubio held talks with External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai on Tuesday. India's foreign ministry said the talks were expected to cover energy, trade, investment and defense, according to the Associated Press report published by KXL. He pointed out that India's foreign minister has been to the United States four times this year, and described India as the most populous country in the world, the largest democracy in the world, an important commercial partner, a defence partner and a key member of the Quad.

"They're a strong strategic partner. I actually don't think we've come enough, and I think we need to have more of them."

— Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State

The optimism in Mumbai follows a long stall. The Associated Press reported that New Delhi and Washington are seeking to revive negotiations stalled for months by tensions over U.S. tariffs and India's purchases of Russian oil. Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50% on most Indian goods in August 2025 after trade talks broke down. Under a framework agreed in February 2026 the tariff rate was reduced to 18%, but negotiations have since stalled. Earlier this month Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks had plateaued, while Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said last week that the first tranche of a trade deal was in its final stages. India says its final tariff rate should be similar to those of competing manufacturing countries such as Vietnam.

One obstacle was eased days before the visit. Hindu BusinessLine reported that President Donald Trump last Friday waived potential tariffs that would have punished New Delhi for its purchases of Russian crude, under legislation he signed in September authorising tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil. Rubio has said the effort to finalise a trade deal was a factor in that waiver decision, and that the administration was entering a 60-day review period to consider what new tariffs, if any, to impose.

Energy featured in the Mumbai remarks as well, but as a supporting item on this visit rather than the headline. Rubio said the U.S. delegation would discuss Venezuelan oil with Reliance and that India had made substantial progress diversifying its oil purchases; a separate report covers that energy discussion in full.

For businesses on both sides, the value of Tuesday's remarks is the timetable language, not a new term sheet. Rubio named no remaining items, gave no date, and announced no agreement. Indian exporters, and diaspora-owned U.S. firms importing from India, still face the framework rate described by the Associated Press until a deal is executed.

What happens next is the announcement Rubio predicted: if the remaining items are wrapped up, an announcement fairly soon, followed by a signing by the leaders.
